transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hey, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so I guess I came in because I just feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like, especially when I'm in the radiology suite or in my classes. Actually, the chairs in my anatomy lecture are the absolute worst. They have those tiny little desks attached to them, you know? The ones that barely fit a notebook, let alone a laptop, and my laptop is this huge gaming rig because I like to play Valorant between my clinical shifts—I'm actually trying to rank up to Ascendant right now, it's been a massive grind and my team keeps throwing. 

But anyway, what was I... right, sitting still. Yeah, after months of just trying to tough it out and just stay in my seat like everyone else, I still end up pacing around the control room, or shifting constantly, or just finding literally any random excuse to get up and move. I just can't stay put.

How far back does this feeling of not being able to sit still go? Has it been something you've dealt with since you were a kid, or is this more of a recent thing that started in college or medical school?

Oh, it goes way, way back. Like, my parents still talk about my elementary school parent-teacher conferences. The teachers were always telling them I was constantly out of my seat, calling out answers, or just rushing ahead on worksheets before they even finished giving the directions. So it was happening way before middle school, definitely not just something that started with my radiology training. 

Actually, speaking of elementary school, do you remember those giant rainbow parachutes we used to play with in gym class? Man, those were the absolute best. We’d all lift it up and run underneath, and it felt like being inside a weird colorful tent. Gym was the only class I actually liked because we could just go crazy, though I got in trouble once for climbing the folded-up bleachers. They look exactly like giant stairs, how are you *not* supposed to climb them, right? I think the gym teacher blew his whistle right in my ear that time. My ears were ringing for like an hour. 

But yeah... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, how long it's been happening. Yeah, definitely since I was a little kid.

Beyond just the physical restlessness you've described, has this difficulty sitting still actually caused problems for you—like affecting your grades, your relationships, or your ability to complete tasks that require focus?

Yeah, it's actually getting really bad. Like, my clinical evaluations have taken a massive hit lately. They even put me on this formal remediation plan, which sounds like something out of a sci-fi movie, right? Like "commence remediation." I was watching *Dune* the other night, have you seen it? The sound design in that movie is absolutely insane, it literally vibrates your chest when you watch it in IMAX. I spent like three hours watching behind-the-scenes videos on how they made the sand worm sounds. They used, like, a microphone buried in actual sand or something crazy like that. I really want to upgrade my gaming headset to get that kind of bass for Valorant. 

But wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the clinic stuff. Yeah, the remediation plan. My supervisors are saying my behavior disrupts the patient flow and makes teamwork way harder. Because I'm always pacing around or just... not standing exactly where I'm supposed to be when they need me to prep the room. Like last week, we had this portable chest X-ray up in the ICU, and those portable machines are basically like driving a giant electric shopping cart. They are so heavy, and the front wheels always squeak. I actually tried spraying WD-40 on one once because the noise was driving me crazy, but the hospital maintenance guy got super mad at me. 

Anyway... yeah, I’m just really worried it could cost me my place in the program if I don’t get it under control. So it's definitely causing some real problems right now.

When you're trying to focus on something—like reading a textbook chapter or watching a lecture—do you find it hard to keep your attention on it, or do you find yourself getting distracted easily, even when you're not feeling restless?

Um, reading a textbook? No, honestly, I don't really have a problem with that. Like, if I'm reading something, I can usually just read it. It's more about the physical part, you know? Just sitting there. Like, my eyes work fine, my brain reads the words, but my body is just... vibrating. 

Speaking of vibrating, did you know that cats purr at a frequency that actually promotes bone healing? I read that somewhere on Reddit. It's like 25 to 140 Hertz or something. I was thinking about that the other day in the clinic when we were doing a bone scan on this guy's tibia. Like, imagine if instead of casts, they just strapped a bunch of purring cats to your leg. That would be insane. My roommate has a cat, actually. Her name is Sir Meows-a-Lot, which is hilarious because it's a girl cat, but whatever. She always tries to sit on my keyboard when I'm playing Valorant, right when I'm trying to hold an angle with an Operator. It's so annoying, but she's really soft. 

But yeah, anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, focusing. Yeah, no, I don't really get distracted like that, it's just the sitting still part that kills me.

Beyond the restlessness and difficulty sitting still, do you find yourself acting without thinking first? Like interrupting people, making impulsive decisions, or doing risky things without considering the consequences?

Yeah, oh my gosh, all the time. It's actually a huge problem in the clinic right now. Like, when my supervisor is explaining a positioning step for a scan, or if they start asking me a question about the protocol, I'll just jump right in and blurt out the answer before they're even done talking. And then, of course, I realize I completely missed the second half of their sentence, which is usually the part that actually mattered. 

It's like my mouth is moving faster than my brain, you know? Sort of like when you're playing a first-person shooter and you just start spraying bullets before you even have your crosshairs on the guy. I play a lot of Valorant, I think I mentioned that. I main Jett, mostly because her movement abilities are so fast. You can literally just dash into a site and cause absolute chaos. My friend Dave always yells at me because I'll dash in without waiting for him to throw his flashbang first, and then I just get instantly headshot. Dave's actually thinking about dropping out of his engineering program to start a Twitch channel, which I think is a terrible idea, but he bought this ridiculous $400 microphone for it. It has this crazy RGB lighting that syncs up with his gameplay. 

Wait, what was the question? Something about acting without thinking? Yeah, so, the blurting things out before my supervisors finish talking. That definitely happens a lot. I just can't seem to wait my turn to speak.

When you're working on a task that requires sustained attention—like studying for an exam or reading through a patient's imaging report—do you find yourself losing track of what you're doing, forgetting what you just read, or having trouble organizing your thoughts? Or is it really just the physical restlessness that's the main issue?

Honestly, no. Reading the reports or studying is fine. I don't forget what I just read or anything like that, and my thoughts are pretty organized. It's really just the physical stuff. Like, if I'm reading a report, my brain is totally focused on the words, but my knee is just bouncing a million miles an hour under the desk. 

I actually wore a hole straight through the bottom of my favorite pair of sneakers just from rubbing my foot against the metal leg of the desk in the radiology reading room. They were these limited edition Nike Dunks, too. The Panda ones. I was so mad. The resale value on those is crazy right now, like way more than I can afford on a student budget. I tried to use this special shoe glue to fix the sole, but it looked terrible and smelled like super strong chemicals. It actually gave my roommate Dave a massive headache, so I had to leave them out on our balcony to air out, and then it randomly downpoured that night. They got completely soaked. So that was a total disaster. I just ended up throwing them away. 

But anyway... wait, did I answer your question? Yeah, no, I don't really lose track of what I'm doing when I have to read or study. My focus is fine, it's just my body that won't chill out.

When you're organizing your study materials or trying to plan out your day, do you find it hard to get started, keep things organized, or remember what you're supposed to do—or does that kind of planning and organizing come pretty naturally to you?

No, getting started and organizing stuff isn't really an issue for me. I actually like planning things out, it's pretty natural. Like, I have this whole color-coded system for my clinic schedule and my classes. It works great. I use Google Calendar, mostly because you can sync it with everything. 

Speaking of Google, did you know they started out in a garage? Like, literally just a rented garage in California. It's crazy to think about. I was watching this documentary about Silicon Valley the other day, and it's wild how many huge tech companies started that way. Apple, Amazon, HP. It makes me feel like I should be doing something more productive with my garage back home. Right now, it's just full of my dad's old woodworking tools that he never uses. He bought this massive table saw like five years ago because he was going to build custom birdhouses, but he made exactly one birdhouse and then gave up because a squirrel moved into it instead of a bird. The squirrel was actually super aggressive, it would throw acorns at our dog. Our dog is a golden retriever, so he's basically completely harmless, he just wanted to be friends with it. 

But yeah, wait, what were you asking? Oh, planning and organizing. Yeah, no, I'm good at that. I don't forget what I'm supposed to do or have trouble starting things. It's just the sitting still part that's the problem.

Back when you were in elementary school—beyond just being out of your seat—did your teachers ever complain that you were forgetful, that you lost things, or that you had trouble paying attention to what they were saying? Or was it really just the hyperactivity part that was the main issue back then?

Honestly, it wasn't the forgetful stuff. My parents still talk about those elementary school conferences where my teachers would just complain that I was always out of my seat, calling out answers, or rushing ahead before they even finished giving the directions. So that kind of thing was happening way before middle school, definitely not just since I started this radiology training. 

But man, those conferences... my parents used to take me to get pizza after them, assuming the teacher didn't say I was totally out of control that week. We always went to this local place that had a massive arcade in the back. I used to spend all my quarters on Time Crisis. Have you ever played that? It's that arcade shooter game where you have a little pedal on the floor you step on to pop out from behind cover. I used to just mash the pedal constantly because I couldn't stand staying hidden. The plastic guns there were always super sticky, though, which is honestly so gross to think about now. 

Especially with all the infection control protocols we have to learn for the hospital. Like, the amount of bacteria on a public arcade gun has to be absolutely astronomical. We actually swabbed our cell phones for a microbiology lab last semester just to see what would grow, and my roommate Dave's phone grew this massive fuzzy green colony that smelled like sour milk. The professor was actually kind of impressed, but I refused to let Dave put his phone on our kitchen counter after that. We had to buy a giant pack of Clorox wipes just for his electronics. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, elementary school. Yeah, no, I didn't really lose my stuff or forget what I was supposed to be doing. It was pretty much just the being out of my seat and rushing ahead part.

When you're doing something you find really interesting—like playing Valorant or watching a movie—can you focus on that for hours without getting distracted, or do you find yourself jumping between different things even when you're enjoying what you're doing?

Honestly, I don't really know about jumping between things. Like, if I'm playing Valorant, I guess I can focus? But even then, I'm always fidgeting or bouncing my leg. Speaking of Valorant, they just dropped this new skin bundle, and the animations are insane. It's got this dragon theme, and when you reload, the dragon actually breathes fire. It's so cool, but it's like eighty bucks, which is a total scam. 

My friend Sarah bought it immediately, though. She works at this high-end coffee shop downtown, so she makes crazy tips. I went there once to study, but it was way too quiet. Like, uncomfortably quiet. And they charge like seven dollars for a plain black coffee. I ended up spilling half of it on my laptop anyway because I couldn't stop tapping my foot against the table leg and bumped the cup. It was a total nightmare. The keys were sticky for a month, and I had to watch all these YouTube tutorials on how to take the keyboard apart using a guitar pick. I don't even play guitar, so I had to buy a pack of picks from the music store down the street. The guy working there was so weird, he kept trying to sell me a ukulele. 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, focusing on games and stuff. Yeah, I'm not really sure if I get distracted or not. I've never really paid attention to that part.

He bought this massive table saw like five years ago because he was going to build custom birdhouses, but he made exactly one birdhouse and then gave up because a squirrel moved into it instead of a bird. The squirrel was actually super aggressive, it would throw acorns at our dog. Our dog is a golden retriever, so he's basically completely harmless, he just wanted to be friends with it. 

But yeah, wait, what were you asking? Oh, planning and organizing. Yeah, no, I'm good at that. I don't forget what I'm supposed to do or have trouble starting things. It's just the sitting still part that's the problem.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had significant problems with inattention and forgetfulness in childhood, which would help confirm ADHD Combined or Predominantly Inattentive presentation versus Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive presentation
doctor.question: Back when you were in elementary school—beyond just being out of your seat—did your teachers ever complain that you were forgetful, that you lost things, or that you had trouble paying attention to what they were saying? Or was it really just the hyperactivity part that was the main issue back then?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My parents still talk about elementary school conferences where teachers said I was always out of my seat, calling out, or rushing ahead before directions were finished. That was happening way before middle school, not just since radiology training.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my behavior in elementary school to determine if my symptoms were present before age 12.

patient.answer:
Honestly, it wasn't the forgetful stuff. My parents still talk about those elementary school conferences where my teachers would just complain that I was always out of my seat, calling out answers, or rushing ahead before they even finished giving the directions. So that kind of thing was happening way before middle school, definitely not just since I started this radiology training. 

But man, those conferences... my parents used to take me to get pizza after them, assuming the teacher didn't say I was totally out of control that week. We always went to this local place that had a massive arcade in the back. I used to spend all my quarters on Time Crisis. Have you ever played that? It's that arcade shooter game where you have a little pedal on the floor you step on to pop out from behind cover. I used to just mash the pedal constantly because I couldn't stand staying hidden. The plastic guns there were always super sticky, though, which is honestly so gross to think about now. 

Especially with all the infection control protocols we have to learn for the hospital. Like, the amount of bacteria on a public arcade gun has to be absolutely astronomical. We actually swabbed our cell phones for a microbiology lab last semester just to see what would grow, and my roommate Dave's phone grew this massive fuzzy green colony that smelled like sour milk. The professor was actually kind of impressed, but I refused to let Dave put his phone on our kitchen counter after that. We had to buy a giant pack of Clorox wipes just for his electronics. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, elementary school. Yeah, no, I didn't really lose my stuff or forget what I was supposed to be doing. It was pretty much just the being out of my seat and rushing ahead part.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has symptoms of inattention/distractibility that would support ADHD Combined Type versus Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type. The patient has consistently denied attention problems, but I need to probe more carefully about whether they actually struggle with sustained attention in less structured environments, or whether they genuinely have intact attention as they claim.
doctor.question: When you're doing something you find really interesting—like playing Valorant or watching a movie—can you focus on that for hours without getting distracted, or do you find yourself jumping between different things even when you're enjoying what you're doing?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining attention during leisure activities (getting distracted or jumping between things), which corresponds to inattentive symptoms. My profile only contains hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, and not difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
Honestly, I don't really know about jumping between things. Like, if I'm playing Valorant, I guess I can focus? But even then, I'm always fidgeting or bouncing my leg. Speaking of Valorant, they just dropped this new skin bundle, and the animations are insane. It's got this dragon theme, and when you reload, the dragon actually breathes fire. It's so cool, but it's like eighty bucks, which is a total scam. 

My friend Sarah bought it immediately, though. She works at this high-end coffee shop downtown, so she makes crazy tips. I went there once to study, but it was way too quiet. Like, uncomfortably quiet. And they charge like seven dollars for a plain black coffee. I ended up spilling half of it on my laptop anyway because I couldn't stop tapping my foot against the table leg and bumped the cup. It was a total nightmare. The keys were sticky for a month, and I had to watch all these YouTube tutorials on how to take the keyboard apart using a guitar pick. I don't even play guitar, so I had to buy a pack of picks from the music store down the street. The guy working there was so weird, he kept trying to sell me a ukulele. 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, focusing on games and stuff. Yeah, I'm not really sure if I get distracted or not. I've never really paid attention to that part.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms beginning in elementary school, with prominent features including chronic inability to sit still, constant fidgeting, frequent interrupting, and impulsive verbal behavior. Core inattention symptoms (forgetfulness, losing things, difficulty sustaining attention to tasks, organizational problems) are notably absent. Functional impairment is significant and documented (clinical remediation plan, supervisor concerns about disrupting patient flow). The symptom pattern is predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type with minimal inattentive features, meeting criteria for ADHD, Combined or Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type. The patient's tangential speech and difficulty maintaining conversational focus during the interview itself further support the diagnosis, though these appear secondary to the hyperactivity-impulsivity rather than primary inattention deficits.
